food.text: Australia became a collection of British colonies from 1788 to 1900, and British and Irish migrants strongly shaped local tastes. Beef cattle, sheep and wheat became staples of the colonial diet.
The Australian gold rushes brought more varied immigrants and cuisines, mainly Italian and Chinese. This began to broaden a diet that had been strongly British and Irish in character.
Chinese migrants numbers exploded with the gold rushes of the 19th century in Australia. By 1890, a third of all cooks in the country were Chinese.

Chinese emigrants first came to New Zealand in 1842, but significant immigration only followed the Otago gold rush in the 1860s. When the gold ran out, many who stayed ran grocery stores and market gardens, and some opened restaurants. The first restaurant selling Chinese food opened in Dunedin during the gold rush era.

The 19th century English botanist Joseph Dalton Hooker remarked that Australian native food plants were "eatable" but not "fit to eat". In 1889, botanist Joseph Maiden agreed, calling them "nothing to boast of as eatables."

Colonisation beginning in 1788 severely affected the traditional use of bush foods by Indigenous Australians. Introduced non-native organisms, along with the loss and destruction of traditional lands and habitats, reduced Aboriginal people's access to native foods.

Most early Chinese migrants to Australia came from Guangdong province, so Cantonese cuisine became the chief influence. Cooks used locally available vegetables and more meat than was usual in traditional recipes.

Early Chinese settlers in New Zealand brought their own fruit and vegetable crops, such as Chinese cabbages, mustard greens, radishes and chrysanthemum. Meat was eaten only on special occasions in China, but its relative affordability meant it was eaten more often, with pork the most favoured.

Ships of whalers brought new crops to Māori communities in the 1800s. Around 1819, an American whaler introduced a larger North American sweet potato to Bay of Plenty Māori, and it became known as the merikana, meaning American. Most traditional kūmara cultivars were mostly supplanted in the 1800s by American varieties.

New Zealand Chinese restaurants often modified their food to attract European customers, sometimes serving fish and chips and steak. At home, many Chinese kept their culinary traditions, most notably splitting and roasting whole pigs inside purpose-built ovens on special occasions. Kau yuk, normally made with taro, was often made with beetroot instead.

The Granny Smith variety of apple originated in Sydney, Australia in 1868. Australia also has large fruit-growing regions, and regional cuisines commonly use locally grown vegetables based on seasonal availability.

Kūmara became less important once potatoes arrived with Western sailors in the 1780s. The potato could grow in colder climates and was considered noa, not tapu, so it could be grown by women or slaves. This shows how sacred rules shaped who farmed which crop.

Sweet potato had been a staple in New Zealand for centuries. In the early 19th century, traditional cultivars there began to be replaced by hardier and larger varieties from the Americas. This happened later in New Zealand than in central Polynesia, where it began by the 17th century.
The first monograph on the flora of Australia noted the lack of edible plants on its first page. It described Billardiera scandens as "almost the only wild eatable fruit of the country".

The waina variety of sweet potato was introduced in the 1850s by a whaler who had come from Rarotonga. Unlike the traditional Māori method of root planting, it was propagated by vine cuttings. This method is the source of the variety's name, since waina means vine.

art.text: Several professional natural-history illustrators accompanied expeditions in the early 19th century. Ferdinand Bauer travelled with Matthew Flinders, and Charles-Alexandre Lesueur travelled with a French expedition led by Nicolas Baudin.

The Victorian gold rush from 1851 brought a huge influx of settlers and new wealth. Even so, the colonial art market mainly wanted landscape paintings, commissioned by wealthy landowners or merchants who wanted to record their material success.

With the gold rushes of the mid-19th century, major buildings went up in the Victorian style, largely in Melbourne and Sydney. Some also appeared in regional capitals such as Ballarat and Bendigo. From about 1850 to 1893, Italianate architecture was also popular because it allowed greater displays of prosperity.

The Art Gallery of New South Wales began as the New South Wales Academy of Art, co-founded by Eliezer Levi Montefiore in 1872. Its first public exhibition opened in 1874, and it was officially opened as the Art Gallery of New South Wales on 22 September 1880.

art.text: Conrad Martens worked as a professional artist from 1835 to 1878 and was commercially successful. His work has been regarded as softening the landscape to fit European sensibilities, and his watercolour studies of Sydney Harbour are well regarded.
S. T. Gill, who lived from 1818 to 1880, documented life on the Australian gold fields. His subject matter stood apart from the landscapes that wealthy patrons mostly wanted to buy.

William Barak, born around 1824, was one of the last traditionally educated Wurundjeri-Willam people from the Melbourne district. His artworks recorded traditional Aboriginal ways for the education of Westerners, and they remain on permanent exhibition at the Ian Potter Centre of the National Gallery of Victoria and the Ballarat Fine Art Gallery.

John Lewin arrived in 1800 as the first resident professional artist in Australia, and he published two volumes of natural history art. Ornithologist John Gould later became renowned for his illustrations of the country's birds.

Gothic Revival architecture gained favour in 19th-century Australia, particularly in churches. Pointed arches, turrets and battlements also appeared on banks, insurance offices, university buildings and homes. One of the best examples is at the lower end of Collins Street in Melbourne.

Conrad Martens is also remembered for accompanying the scientist Charles Darwin on HMS Beagle, as had Augustus Earle. His Sydney Harbour watercolours are seen as introducing Romantic ideals to his painting.

Italianate style was pushed to an extreme by some architects toward the end of the century. Buildings became over-burdened with excess columns, balustrades and exaggerated entrances. Medley Hall in Carlton is an example of this Boom Style, which lasted from 1880 to 1893.

The gallery's collection began in 1871 with large European works such as Ford Madox Brown's Chaucer at the Court of Edward III. It later bought Australian works including Streeton's 1891 Fire's On, Roberts' 1894 The Golden Fleece and McCubbin's 1896 On the Wallaby Track.

war.text: The Battle of the Eureka Stockade was fought in Ballarat, Victoria, on 3 December 1854, between gold miners and the colonial forces. It was the culmination of the 1851–1854 Eureka Rebellion during the Victorian gold rush. The fighting left at least 27 dead and many injured, most of them rebels. Most of the killing came after the rebels' resistance had slackened: government forces bayoneted the wounded and targeted non-combatants, and a woman was reportedly butchered by a mounted trooper while pleading for her husband's life.

From the 1830s settlers spread rapidly through inland eastern Australia, and widespread conflict followed. Across the Liverpool Plains, 16 British and up to 500 Indigenous Australians were killed between 1832 and 1838. The violence included several massacres of Indigenous people.

The Black War of 1828–1832 and the Black Line of 1830 were turning points for Aboriginal Tasmanians and European settlers. Martial law was declared against the Aboriginal people, bounties of £5 for an adult and £2 for a child were offered for capturing those without passes, and this often led to organised hunts that ended in deaths. Many Aboriginal people avoided capture, but they were shaken by the size of the campaigns against them and became willing to surrender to Robinson and move to Flinders Island. Many Aboriginal deaths went unrecorded, and the number of Aboriginal people shot is likely a substantial undercount.

The Second Boer War, fought from 1899 to 1902, marked the largest overseas deployment of Australia's colonial forces. It came just as the separate colonies were federating into the Commonwealth of Australia in 1901.

Violence on the Liverpool Plains included several massacres of Indigenous people, among them the Waterloo Creek massacre and the Myall Creek massacres in 1838. In the fighting on the plains between 1832 and 1838, 16 British and up to 500 Indigenous Australians were killed. The violence did not end until 1843, and further violence followed in the New England region during the early 1840s.

The British settlement of Fort Dundas on Melville Island was established in 1824 as an early military outpost in northern Australia. It was abandoned in 1829 because of attacks from the local Tiwi people. Fighting also took place near Fort Wellington on the Cobourg Peninsula between 1827 and 1829.

Before the Eureka Stockade, the Bendigo Petition gathered over 5,000 signatures and was presented to Lieutenant-Governor Charles La Trobe in August 1853. Later, a judicial enquiry into the murder of miner James Scobie outside the Eureka Hotel found no guilt in the owner, James Bently, who was deeply suspected of involvement, and the case was presided over by a police magistrate accused of a conflict of interest. The outcome helped the "physical force" faction gain the upper hand over those favouring "moral force".

Free settlement of Queensland began in 1838, and from 1840 a great rush for land in areas such as the Darling Downs and Brisbane Valley led to widespread fighting with heavy loss of life. The conflict later spread north to the Wide Bay and Burnett River region, and at one stage the settlement of Maryborough was virtually under siege. Both sides committed atrocities: settlers poisoned a large number of Indigenous people, for example at Kilcoy in 1842 and on Whiteside near Brisbane in 1847, and each of those poisonings was said to have taken up to 70 Aboriginal lives, using flour laced with strychnine.

Settlers poisoned a large number of Indigenous people at Kilcoy in 1842; the massacre was said to have taken up to 70 Aboriginal lives, through a gift of flour laced with strychnine. In retaliation, Multuggerah and his warriors ambushed a group of settlers at the Battle of One Tree Hill in September 1843. They routed that group and then others in the skirmishes that followed.

A wide variety of weapons were used at Eureka, including Colt revolvers, pepperbox revolvers, horse pistols, Bowie knives, swords and pikes. The government forces used the Lovell 1842 pattern smooth bore muzzle-loading musket.

After the Black War and removal to Flinders Island, the number of Aboriginal Tasmanians kept falling. Of the 220 who arrived with Robinson at Wybalenna, most died in the following 14 years from introduced disease and inadequate shelter, and few children survived infancy. Numbers were estimated at a dozen in 1859, and by 1869 only one remained, who died in 1876.

Captain John Thomas' interim report for the 12th and 40th Regiments listed one soldier killed in action, two died of wounds and fourteen wounded. Private James Hammond died of his wounds after the battle, on the way to Geelong. Historian Gregory Blake estimates military casualties were more likely around 30, since men with slight injuries went unreported.

literature.text: In 1838 Anna Maria Bunn's The Guardian: a tale was published in Sydney. It was the first Australian novel printed and published in mainland Australia, and the first Australian novel written by a woman. It is a Gothic romance.
Ethel Turner's Seven Little Australians follows the adventures of seven mischievous children in Sydney. It has been in print since 1894, longer than any other Australian children's novel.
In 1823 explorer and author William Charles Wentworth published Australasia. It was the first book of verse by a native-born Australian poet, and it espoused his ideals of Australian identity.
Henry Handel Richardson's The Getting of Wisdom (1910) is about an unconventional schoolgirl in Melbourne. It has enjoyed lasting success and has been praised by H. G. Wells and Germaine Greer.
Poetry played an important part in early Australian literature. Charles Harpur and Henry Kendall are described as the first poets of any consequence.

The Australian Magazine, which ran from June 1821 to May 1822, was the first periodical that could be called a literary journal in Australia. It featured poetry, a two-part story and articles on theology and general topics.

Most 19th-century literary journals after The Australian Magazine were based in Sydney or Melbourne, and few lasted long. They struggled with a lack of capital, the small local market and competition from literary journals from Britain.

James Unaipon (c.1835-1907) contributed to accounts of Ngarrindjeri mythology written by the missionary George Taplin in South Australia. His son David Unaipon later provided the first accounts of Aboriginal mythology written by an Aboriginal person.

science.text: Sydney Observatory was built between 1857 and 1859 on Observatory Hill in Sydney, on a site that had previously held a fort and a signal station. Its historic 29-centimetre refractor telescope, built in 1874, remains the oldest telescope in Australia still in regular use.

William Farrer, an English-born agronomist, emigrated to Australia in 1870 after earning a bachelor of arts degree at Cambridge in 1868. He suffered from tuberculosis and hoped Australia's drier, warmer climate would be better for his delicate health. He spent decades breeding wheat, and his work earned him the title 'father of the Australian wheat industry.'

The Great Melbourne Telescope was built by the Grubb Telescope Company in Dublin in 1868 and installed at the Melbourne Observatory in 1869. With a 48-inch primary mirror, it was one of the largest telescopes in the world at the time.

Lawrence Hargrave, an English-born engineer who immigrated to Australia in 1865, is best known for inventing the box kite, which went on to form the aerodynamic basis of early biplanes. He deliberately never patented any of his inventions, believing scientific communication mattered more than profit.

Ernest Rutherford, a New Zealand-born physicist and chemist later called 'the father of nuclear physics,' studied at Canterbury College in Christchurch, part of the University of New Zealand, between 1890 and 1894. In 1895 he won a scholarship that took him to Cambridge University's Cavendish Laboratory for postgraduate study.

William Scott was appointed Sydney Observatory's first Government Astronomer in 1856, and the new building was completed in 1858. It was designed by Colonial Architect Alexander Dawson and built by Charles Bingemann and Ebenezer Dewar.

Farrer worked for the New South Wales Department of Lands in wheat-growing districts from 1875 to 1886, then became a wheat experimentalist with the NSW Department of Agriculture in 1898. He crossed varieties such as Canadian Fife and Purple Straw to combine their best qualities.

On 12 November 1894, Hargrave lifted himself 16 feet off the ground at Stanwell Park Beach using a train of four box kites in a 21 mile-per-hour wind. Aided by caretaker James Swain, he carried an anemometer and clinometer to measure the wind speed and the kite line's angle.

Henry Chamberlain Russell served as Sydney Observatory's Government Astronomer from 1870 until his death in 1907, during which time the observatory took some of the first astronomical photographs of the southern sky. In 1899 it also began work on the international Astrographic Catalogue, a project that eventually filled 53 volumes.

In 1900 Farrer finally achieved a rust-resistant, high-yielding wheat strain, and by 1903 his 'Federation' wheat, named for the recent Federation of Australia, was released to farmers. Over the next 20 years it helped treble Australia's wheat harvest.

A western wing was added to Sydney Observatory in 1877, providing office and library space along with a second dome for another telescope. This expansion came during the long tenure of Government Astronomer Henry Chamberlain Russell, who held the post from 1870 to 1907.

politics.text: The South Australia Act, 1834 created the Province of South Australia, built on the principles of systematic colonisation. It forbade convict settlers, even though convicts were being sent to other colonies at the time.

In 1910, the government of John Verran in South Australia served as the first complete Labor party government in the world. It came only nine years after South Australia became a state of the Commonwealth of Australia.

The Australian Colonies Government Act 1850 was a landmark law that granted representative constitutions to New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia and Tasmania. The colonies wrote democratically progressive parliaments with the British monarch as symbolic head of state.

The Commonwealth of Australia was proclaimed on 1 January 1901 as a federation of six self-governing former British colonies. The name was formalised in the Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act 1900 (UK).

In 1840 Royal Navy officer William Hobson and several Māori chiefs signed the Treaty of Waitangi, which transformed New Zealand into a colony of the British Empire and made all Māori British subjects. Tensions over settler encroachment on Māori lands and disputes over land sales led to the New Zealand Wars (1845 to 1872) between the colonial government and the Māori. In response to the conflict, the colonial government carried out a series of land confiscations from the Māori. This upheaval, combined with epidemics of infectious diseases from Europe, devastated the Māori population and their social standing.

South Australia became a self-governing colony in 1857 with the ratification of the Constitution Act 1856, and the Parliament of South Australia was formed. This followed the South Australia Act 1842, which had given the British Government full control after the colony nearly went bankrupt.

The secret ballot was adopted in Tasmania, Victoria and South Australia in 1856, followed by New South Wales in 1858, Queensland in 1859 and Western Australia in 1877. South Australia also introduced universal male suffrage for its lower house in 1856.

In 1890, a strike in the shipping industry spread to wharves, railways, mines and shearing sheds. Employers locked out workers and used non-union labour, and colonial governments intervened with police and troops. The strike failed, as did shearers' strikes in 1891 and 1894.
Lachlan Macquarie, the last autocratic Governor of New South Wales, served from 1810 to 1821. He upset British government opinion by treating emancipists as equal to free settlers.

George Reid, leader of the Free Trade Party from 1901 to 1905, imagined an Australian political spectrum running from socialist to anti-socialist. He tried to reframe the party system this way. In 1909 the Free Trade and Protectionist parties merged to form the Commonwealth Liberal Party to oppose the new Labor Party.
Queensland excluded Aboriginal males from voting in 1885. In Western Australia, a property qualification for voting existed for male Aboriginals, Asians, Africans and people of mixed descent.
Governor Lachlan Macquarie recommended the name Australia to replace New Holland in December 1817. The British Admiralty adopted it in 1824, and the British Parliament used it in legislation in 1828.

Attorney general John Plunkett twice charged colonists responsible for the Myall Creek massacre of Aboriginal people with murder, resulting in a conviction. His Church Act of 1836 disestablished the Church of England and established legal equality between Anglicans, Catholics and Presbyterians.

William Wentworth was a statesman, pastoralist, explorer, newspaper editor, lawyer, politician and author. With Gregory Blaxland and William Lawson he led the 1813 crossing of the Blue Mountains, the first by non-Aboriginal people.

After the 1910 elections, Labor won a majority in both houses and Fisher again became prime minister. His government introduced a progressive land tax, invalid pensions and a maternity allowance, and established the Commonwealth Bank in 1911. It also took over the Northern Territory from South Australia in 1911.

philosophy.text: Australia's earliest academic philosophers were appointed in the late nineteenth century. Like their European contemporaries, most were idealists. They included Sir Francis Anderson, professor of philosophy at Sydney University from 1890 to 1921, W. R. Boyce Gibson in Melbourne, and, to a degree, Sir William Mitchell in Adelaide.

Aboriginal Australian religion and mythology was the prevalent belief system in Australia until around 1840. That was when European Australians first outnumbered Indigenous Australians. Afterwards, Australia was for a period majority Protestant, with a large Catholic minority.

The Church of England originally held a position of privilege in early colonial Australia. The Church Act 1836, drafted by reformist attorney-general John Plunkett, disestablished it in New South Wales. The act gave legal equality to Anglicans, Catholics and Presbyterians, and was later extended to Methodists.

By 1901, apart from the Indigenous population and descendants of gold rush migrants, Australian society was predominantly Anglo-Celtic. Some 40% of the population was Anglican, 23% Catholic and 34% other Christian. About 1% professed non-Christian religions.

Freedom of religion was enshrined in Section 116 of the Constitution of Australia of 1901. The Australian Constitution guaranteed the separation of church and state. Section 116 bars the Commonwealth from establishing any religion or requiring a religious test for public office.

Smaller religious groups also arrived and established churches. Jews began arriving in the early 19th century. British Nonconformist Methodists, Presbyterians, Congregationalists and Baptists set up their own churches, as did Lutherans from Germany.

The first Catholic priests arrived in Australia as convicts in 1800. The Castle Hill Rebellion of 1804 alarmed the British authorities, and no further priests were allowed in the colony until 1820. In that year London sent John Joseph Therry and Philip Connolly.

Afghan cameleers helped establish the Muslim faith in Australia. The Marree Mosque, the first mosque in Australia, was built by them in the 19th century. The Adelaide Mosque, built in 1888 to 1889, is the oldest permanent mosque in Australia.

The Point McLeay Mission was established in 1860 by the Aborigines' Friends Association, an interdenominational Christian missionary group. Its goal was to convert the surviving Ngarrindjeri to Christianity and train them for domestic labour. By the time David Unaipon was born in 1872, the Ngarrindjeri had been decimated by disease and displaced from their land. Their population had been reduced from an estimated 8,000 in 1834 to just 2,000 by 1860.

In 1909 David Unaipon toured Adelaide with the Point McLeay Mission's Glee Club. He spoke to audiences about Indigenous knowledge of astronomy and botany, and about Ngarrindjeri traditions and folklore. The press labelled him "Australia's Leonardo" and a "black genius".

culture.text: A famous Australian victory on the 1882 tour of England led to a satirical obituary in an English newspaper. It said English cricket had "died" and that the "body will be cremated and the ashes taken to Australia". The English media then dubbed the 1882–83 tour a quest to "regain the ashes".

Hobart's Theatre Royal opened in 1837 and is Australia's oldest continuously operating theatre. Adelaide's Queen's Theatre, established in 1841, is today the oldest purpose-built theatre on the mainland.

The 1876–77 season is notable for a match at the Melbourne Cricket Ground between a combined XI from New South Wales and Victoria and a touring English team. That match was later recognised as the first Test match.
The first recorded cricket match in Australia took place in Sydney in 1803. Intercolonial contests started in 1851, and Sheffield Shield inter-state cricket continues to this day.
The mid-19th-century gold rushes provided funds for the construction of grand theatres in the Victorian style. One example was the Princess Theatre in Melbourne, established in 1854.

The first Afghan cameleers arrived in Melbourne in June 1860. Three men came with a shipment of 24 camels for the Burke and Wills expedition. They went on to work in the arid interior from the 1860s to the 1930s.

The success of Arthur Comino's fish shop in Sydney gave rise to a chain migration of Greek migrants. By 1900, hundreds of them had opened oyster saloons across Australia, the start of a Greek café tradition.
In 1866–67, prominent cricketer and Australian rules football pioneer Tom Wills coached an Aboriginal cricket team. The team later toured England in 1868 under the captaincy of Charles Lawrence.
The outlaw Ned Kelly (1855-80) achieved the status of a national folk hero. Ballads, films and paintings have since 1878 perpetuated his legend, although he was hanged for murder.
Cameleers were prohibited from bringing their wives to Australia. As a result, the Afghan community during this period was almost entirely made up of men.
